1.pericope_label: A promise being left us: the word preached did not profit them

schools.summary: Begin by objecting to the page rather than the text: there is no break in the argument on the psalm, and this is a poor chapter division. Place the stress within the sentence, on fear and not on us, noting that the writer begins with let us though about to write lest any of you, since he will have gained his object if he brings his readers to share his fear. On the word rendered seem, hold it impossible that the sense can be should even seem, or should think himself to have failed; the writer may be avoiding direct language about what lies beyond mortal ken, but more probably he is drawn on by the figure in the next word, the falling short of a mark, and so refers to the judge who declares the failure — lest any one be adjudged to have come short. On the second verse, say that the change of reading rests on the strongest authority and compels us to connect the words with the people rather than the message, so that speakers and hearers must be united by the bond of faith; but call the phrase very difficult and leave the text uncertain.

Make the exhortation a rule of pastoral care: a good shepherd so watches the flock that no one sheep is lost, and every one ought to fear for his neighbours as well as himself. But fence the word at once, since the fear recommended is not that which shakes the confidence of faith but such as keeps us from growing torpid with indifference, and no one comes short except he who by rejecting grace has first renounced the promise. On the word rendered seem, report that some consider it pleonastic and grant that it sometimes is, but hold it has a special meaning here, the Apostle wishing no one to present even the appearance of neglecting the promised rest. And draw the doctrine from the second verse: the word separated from faith can confer no good — not that its power depends on us, for were the whole world false he who cannot lie would still be true, but it never puts forth its power in us except when faith gives it entrance.

Take the clause plainly, that lest any of us should actually come short means lest we miss it; and hear in the verb an allusion to the Grecian games, of which this epistle has many, since he that came short was any distance, no matter how small, behind the winner. Press that home: will it avail us how near we get to heaven, if the door be shut before we arrive? On the second verse, report that several of the best copies read the participle as agreeing with the people rather than the word, so that they were not mixed with those who heard it by faith, not of the same spirit with Joshua and Caleb, though judge the common text best. Then explain the metaphor by the nutrition of the body, since food received into the stomach and not mixed with the saliva and the gastric juice would be the means of death rather than life; and support the usage from a description of health as a proper mixture of the wet and dry, the cold and hot.

Read the promise as a legacy left us by Christ in his last will and testament, so that our business is to see that we be the legatees, laying claim to that rest and freedom from the dominion of sin by which the souls of men are kept in servitude. Argue from strength rather than from deficiency: the best privileges the ancient Jews had were their gospel privileges, since whatever was excellent in the sacrifices was their respect to Christ, and we have the same gospel in greater purity and perspicuity. Then sharpen the warning — it is a dreadful thing so much as to seem to fall short of the gospel salvation. And name what is at the bottom of all unprofitable hearing: it is our unbelief, for faith in the hearer is the life of the word, and it must be in act and exercise while we are hearing.

debates.question: What does the word rendered 'seem to come short' mean?

sides.position: Nothing qualifying at all: lest any of us should actually come short, that is, miss it
Be adjudged to have come short: the figure of falling short of a mark draws in the judge who witnesses and declares the failure
Some think it pleonastic, but it has a special meaning here — no one should present even the appearance of neglecting the promise

debates.question: Was it the word, or the hearers, that was 'not mixed with faith'?

sides.position: The hearers, on the strongest authority: they were not united by faith with them that heard
Several of the best copies read it so, but the common text seems best — the word was not mixed with faith
The phrase is very difficult and the text uncertain; on the reading which agrees with the people the English translation is correct

outliers.note: Alone explains 'mixed with faith' by physiology, arguing that the most nutritive food not mixed with the saliva and gastric juice would be the means of death rather than life, and supporting the usage from an ancient definition of health as a proper mixture of the wet and dry, the cold and hot.

Alone distinguishes the fear commanded from the fear forbidden — not that which shakes the confidence of faith, but that which keeps us from growing torpid with indifference — and alone turns the exhortation into a duty toward others, that every one should fear for his neighbours as well as for himself.
Alone objects to the chapter division itself, observing that there is no break in the argument on the psalm and calling it a poor division.

themes: Let us therefore fear, lest, a promise being left us of entering into his rest, any of you should seem to come short of it.
For unto us was the gospel preached, as well as unto them: but the word preached did not profit them, not being mixed with faith in them that heard it.

3.pericope_label: We which have believed do enter into rest; God did rest the seventh day

schools.summary: State the aim soberly: the object is not to establish a truth absolutely new but to show that in this Scripture and in that a received truth lies contained; and do not soften the appeal, since the perfect tense carries the permanent value of what was said — God has spoken, and that is enough for us. Find the emphasis of the opening clause two-fold, on believed, which looks back to the faith of the previous verse, and on we enter, which looks forward; and take the present tense as emphatic and futuristic, we are sure to enter in, we who believe. Explain why the caution about creation was needed, that the psalmist's words are drawn from the opening of Genesis, so that though the same words are used the thought is widely different. Then generalise: the notion of rest runs through every dispensation, seen in the finishing of creation, in the appointment of the Sabbath, in the offer of the promised land and now in the promise of heaven — being careful that God's resting does not mean he was wearied, only that he ceased from creation while never ceasing to carry forward the affairs of the universe. Note also that a Jewish writer quotes the same verse with the same mannerism of indefinite citation, and that the seventh day of God's rest was still going on, and so was clearly not a day of twenty-four hours.

Say first what kind of exegesis is being done, since it governs everything after. The writer has hitherto taken the psalm according to the letter, but now amplifies and decorates it, so that he rather alludes to than explains the words of David — an embellishment Paul used before on a saying of Moses, and nothing unsuitable when Scripture is accommodated to the subject in hand. Then lay out what each stage of the reasoning turns on: the word rest, to show the rest meant was not the Sabbath, and then the word to day, to show it was not the rest of Canaan; and call the two short verses following explanatory and parenthetic. Define the true rest of the faithful, which is to continue for ever, as the state in which they shall rest as God did, since the highest happiness of man is to be united to his God. But on the present tense, deny that eternal rest is meant, which is not entered now and cannot be laboured for; the Gospel rest is intended, a rest from the burden of the law and from all toil for salvation by works, lying in much inward peace notwithstanding the world's troubles.

Say that we do actually possess this rest, having peace of conscience and joy in the Holy Ghost and being saved from the guilt and power of sin, these blessings being the forerunners of the eternal glory typified by the earthly felicity promised to Israel. Report the textual state of the clause: the words we who believe are omitted by Chrysostom and a few copies, and several others read therefore let us enter rather than for we do enter, which would answer neatly to therefore let us fear in the first verse; but that reading cannot stand, since the words it requires to be dropped are acknowledged genuine by every manuscript of note. Then state the chain of proof as a bare argument: the psalm mentions a rest, but not God's rest from creating, since that was long before the time of Moses, so that in his time another rest was expected, of which those who then heard fell short.

debates.question: Is the rest that believers enter a present possession or a future certainty?

sides.position: Present: a spiritual rest in Christ now, from the burden of the law and from toil for salvation by works
Future, and certain: the present tense is emphatic and futuristic — we are sure to enter in
The true rest of the faithful, which is to continue for ever, is the state in which they shall rest as God did

outliers.note: Alone characterises the writer's method rather than his conclusion, holding that he has passed from taking the psalm according to the letter to amplifying and decorating it, so that here he rather alludes to than explains David's words; and alone identifies the single particle on which the difficult construction turns.

Alone reports the textual state of the opening clause, including a variant that would make it therefore let us enter, answering to therefore let us fear in the first verse, and alone explains why that attractive reading cannot stand.

Alone draws the inference that the seventh day of God's rest was still going on and so was clearly not a day of twenty-four hours, and alone notes that a Jewish writer cites the same verse with the same literary mannerism of indefinite quotation.

themes: For we which have believed do enter into rest, as he said, As I have sworn in my wrath, if they shall enter into my rest: although the works were finished from the foundation of the world.
For he spake in a certain place of the seventh day on this wise, And God did rest the seventh day from all his works.
And in this place again, If they shall enter into my rest.

6.pericope_label: Again he limiteth a certain day, saying in David, To day

schools.summary: Build the argument the objectors suspect, and build it plainly: it was a settled matter that some would enter, since a rest deserving to be called the rest of God would not be prepared in vain, and as those to whom it was first offered would not enter, it must have been designed for others. Summarise the five particulars the preceding verses establish and find them repeated here; and notice that this verse says disobedience where the second said unbelief, comparing the transition elsewhere from believeth to obeyeth. Explain the verb for limiting as bounding a field and then fixing definitely, so that the writer mentions to day particularly, the object being to show the offer was not confined to those who first received it, since five hundred years later David still speaks of a rest that might be lost by hardening the heart. Take in David to mean the Book of Psalms, though the Greek version ascribes this psalm to him. On the last verse, say there can be no doubt Joshua is intended, and state what the name serves to prove: Joshua did give them a rest in the land, but not all that was intended, and had it been final the matter would not have been alluded to again in David's time. And make an admission the others do not — the argument is rabbinical throughout, though the author is writing to Jews.

State the objection before answering it, since it is the honest difficulty. David's words seem to express no such thing, meaning only that God punished the people's unbelief by refusing them the land. The answer is that the inference holds, for if nothing were promised now the warning would be unsuitable — take heed lest the same thing happen to you as to the fathers — so that as their unbelief deprived them, the promise is renewed to their children. On the day, say that since the seventh day of creation was a rest God entered and not man, and the land of Canaan a typical rest the unbelieving did not enter, he has fixed and appointed a certain day, the Gospel dispensation, for believers to enter into it. Then draw out the type at length: the agreement in the names, both signifying a saviour, the one temporal and the other spiritual; both servants in office; and the correspondence in the battles won, the saving of Rahab, the receiving of the Gibeonites, and the leading of Israel into Canaan to divide it by lot.

Attack the translators before touching the argument. There is no conjecturing why they inserted the word must, and one may hope it was not to serve a system, since some have since used it so — some must go to heaven, for so is the doctrine of the decree, and certain persons must be infallibly brought thither as a reward to Christ for his sufferings, in which the will of man has no part. Supposing all that true, it is not in the text either positively or by implication; literally rendered it says only that it remaineth for some to enter in. Then take the day: the time of rest for the ancient Jews being past and the true rest never enjoyed, God in mercy has instituted another day, so that his voice is in the Gospel as it was in the law. And on the last verse, call it truly surprising that the translators wrote Jesus and not Joshua, since the Greek version everywhere renders the Hebrew name so, and it is that reading the apostle follows; note that one manuscript adds the son of Nave to prevent the wrong application, that Theodoret and a Syriac version do the same, and that Coverdale and Tindal and later English editions read Joshua, as does our own margin — a pity it was not in the text, since the smaller Bibles carry no margin and simple people are bewildered by it.

debates.question: Does the text say that some MUST enter into the rest?

sides.position: No: the word must is an insertion, and the doctrine of the decree some rest on it is not in the text either positively or by implication
It was a settled matter that some would enter, since God would not prepare such a rest in vain and those first offered it refused

debates.question: Is the failure at verse 6 called unbelief or disobedience?

sides.position: Disobedience, though the second verse spoke of unbelief — the transition from believing to obeying is found elsewhere too
Unbelief, which was the cause throughout

outliers.note: Alone attacks the English translators twice in three verses, first over the inserted word must and the doctrine of the decree built on it, then over their writing Jesus where Joshua was meant; and alone lists the earlier English versions that got the name right, regretting that the smaller Bibles carry no margin in which the correction could be seen.
Alone concedes the character of the reasoning, calling it a rabbinical argument all along, while noting that the author is writing to Jews and so may fairly use one.

Alone develops Joshua as a type at length — the shared name meaning saviour, the shared office of servant, the battles, the saving of Rahab, the receiving of the Gibeonites and the dividing of Canaan by lot — where the others use the name only to date the argument.

themes: Seeing therefore it remaineth that some must enter therein, and they to whom it was first preached entered not in because of unbelief:
Again, he limiteth a certain day, saying in David, To day, after so long a time; as it is said, To day if ye will hear his voice, harden not your hearts.
For if Jesus had given them rest, then would he not afterward have spoken of another day.

9.pericope_label: There remaineth therefore a rest to the people of God

schools.summary: Notice that the noun has changed, and let the change carry the argument. The word here is not the ordinary one for a Sabbath but one meaning the keeping of one, occurring nowhere else in the New Testament; and rule out the alternatives in turn. It cannot mean the rest in Canaan, since the whole drift has been to prove otherwise; it cannot mean the Sabbath proper, or the usual word would have been used; it cannot mean the Christian Sabbath, or the reasoning about being excluded by unbelief would be irrelevant. It must therefore mean heaven, and the best description of heaven is to call it an eternal Sabbath — a place where there will be employment without fatigue, where the slave shall rest from his toil and the man broken by anxious care shall cease from his labours. On the tenth verse, mark the symmetry: as God's rest was the goal of the creative work, so this rest is the goal of the life of works for the people of God. Then face the question the whole argument has been inviting, how far this wide meaning is present in the psalm itself, and answer it flatly — we have no right to look on this argument as an accommodation or a mere application of Scripture, since the psalmist pointedly changes the historian's words about the land into words about God's rest, and his language was susceptible of the higher meaning already. On the exhortation, explain the last noun as meaning a copy, and add the plain moral: the Israelites set a terrible example, and it is so easy to copy the bad ones.

Deny that eternal rest is meant, since that is not entered now and cannot be laboured for, salvation not being by works and eternal life being a free gift; the Gospel rest is intended, which believers enter by degrees and enjoy more of by believing, and which is to be laboured for by prayer and hearing and attendance on ordinances. On the tenth verse, argue that the person meant is not the believer but Christ himself, since a single person is spoken of and not many, since the rest entered is his own, which can be said of no other, and since the comparison with God's ceasing from his works fits only him — so that Christ entered his rest not when he was laid in the grave but when he rose and sat down at the right hand of God, and that is the ground and foundation of the saints' rest. Keep the figure of the course through the exhortation, noting that entering into rest is compared to a straight course and falling set in opposition to it.

Decline to choose between the two rests and say you understand it as including both. Read the tenth verse of the believer, who has ceased from his own works in the sense of no longer depending on Mosaic rites for justification, resting from them as fully as God rested from creation; and note that in speaking of the Sabbath as typifying a state of blessedness the apostle follows the opinions of the Jews of his own and after times, among whom the phrase for the sabbath above and the sabbath below was common. On the exhortation, take the verb to imply every exertion of body and mind, all other things omitted that this one thing be done; and draw the conclusion the system requires, that the apostle never supposed a man might not make final shipwreck of faith so long as he was in a state of probation.

State the principle without softening it. Faith is great and brings salvation, and without it none can ever be saved; but it suffices not of itself to accomplish this, there being need of a right conversation also, and of much earnestness, for truly there is need of much earnestness to go up into Heaven. Press the comparison: if they who suffered so great distress in the wilderness were not counted worthy of the land, because they murmured and committed fornication, how shall we be counted worthy of Heaven if we live carelessly and indolently? And observe that the punishment threatened does not stop at failing to enter, since he adds what most of all arouses men, that we should have our mind and hope and expectation yonder, lest we fail.

debates.question: What is the rest that remains for the people of God?

sides.position: Heaven: the word is not the ordinary one for Sabbath, and Canaan, the Sabbath proper and the Christian Sabbath are each excluded in turn
The Gospel rest, which believers enter now by degrees; eternal rest cannot be laboured for, salvation not being by works
Both are included

debates.question: Who is 'he that is entered into his rest' in verse 10?

sides.position: Christ, since a single person is spoken of, the rest entered is his own, and he entered it when he rose and sat down at the right hand of God
The believer, who has ceased from his own works by no longer depending on Mosaic rites for justification

debates.question: Is the argument of this section an accommodation of the Psalm?

sides.position: No: we have no right to call it an accommodation or a mere application, since the Psalmist's own language was susceptible of the higher meaning
The writer amplifies and decorates the Psalm, alluding to rather than explaining David's words, as Scripture may fitly be accommodated to the subject in hand

outliers.note: Alone rests the whole identification on the rare noun, excluding Canaan, the Sabbath and the Christian Sabbath each by a separate argument; and alone develops heaven as an eternal Sabbath in which the slave rests from his toil and the man worn by anxious care ceases from his labours.

Alone reads verse 10 of Christ rather than of the believer, resting it on the singular person, on the rest being called his own, and on the parallel with God's ceasing from his works — so that the saints' rest is grounded on the ascension.

Alone insists that faith, though it brings salvation and none can be saved without it, does not suffice of itself, a right conversation being needed as well; and alone presses the comparison that those who bore such distress in the wilderness still failed of the land.

themes: There remaineth therefore a rest to the people of God.
For he that is entered into his rest, he also hath ceased from his own works, as God did from his.
Let us labour therefore to enter into that rest, lest any man fall after the same example of unbelief.

12.pericope_label: The word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword

schools.summary: State both cases before deciding. Outside John's writings no passage invests the word of God so clearly with personal attributes; there certainly is personification, and the language would, standing alone, suggest a divine Person. But it is not easy to believe the phrase sharper than a two-edged sword would be applied directly to the Son, and this epistle refers repeatedly to the word of God in revelation with no trace of another meaning; the key is its habitual thought of Scripture as a direct divine utterance. Take it therefore as the whole word of God, mainly of threatening but also of promise. Be careful about the Alexandrian parallels too: the resemblances to Philo, who speaks of the divine Word cutting through all things and separating the parts of the soul, are too close to be accidental, but prove familiarity rather than adoption of his system — the author uses Philonic language rather than Philonic ideas. Or decline the question altogether, taking the word of God as what God speaks, promise or threatening, law or gospel, and reading the verse for its purpose, that we cannot escape God's notice. On the imagery, note that the adjective means two-mouthed, the sword being given a mouth because it seemed to devour what was before it, and that the Roman sword was commonly two-edged; and insist on a rendering that changes the sense — it divides soul and spirit, not soul from spirit, severing bone from bone and piercing the marrow, the words transferred by a natural metaphor from the material frame to the soul.

Name the sides of the dispute before taking one, since the fathers and later divines are divided: Augustin and Ambrose and Owen and Doddridge hold the word here to be Christ, Chrysostom and Theophylact and Beza hold it to be Scripture, and the latter is clearly the most suitable, the only difficulty being the verse that follows, where a transition is made from the word of God to God himself. Against that, the case for Christ can be stated firmly: the Word of God was a known name of the Messiah among the Jews, which is why the apostle uses it in writing to them; not a thing but a person is spoken of, a Judge and critical discerner of the secrets of men's hearts, who is said to be a priest in the verses following. Then ask a question none of the others put — whether the effect described belongs to all hearers or only to the faithful — and answer that it must be confined to the faithful, since only they are searched to the quick, hypocrisy sifted and the old man slain by the edge of the spiritual sword; and yet the context shows a general truth, for the reprobate, though they set an iron heart against it, are dragged to the tribunal by the very word they deride, like furious dogs that bite and claw the chain by which they are bound and can do nothing.

Argue against the Christological reading on a single ground of usage: Paul in none of his thirteen acknowledged epistles so denominates our Lord, nor does any New Testament writer except John. Grant that Owen attempted the contrary, but show that his two supporting texts fail. Then quote an authority who concedes everything except the point at issue — that none of the properties named here can be denied to the Son, who sees all things, penetrates all things, rules the heart and turns it where he pleases — and yet denies the Logos is intended, since the conjunction shows the verse is an inference from what precedes about rest.

debates.question: Is 'the word of God' here Christ or the Scripture?

sides.position: Christ, the essential Word: the Word of God was a known name of the Messiah among the Jews, and a person is spoken of, not a thing
Not Christ: Paul never so denominates our Lord in his acknowledged epistles, and the conjunction makes the verse an inference from what precedes about rest
The whole word of God in revelation; there is personification, but the phrase 'sharper than a two-edged sword' could not be applied directly to the Son
Simply what God speaks — promise or threatening, law or gospel; the question need not be settled to read the verse

debates.question: Does the word work this effect on all hearers, or only on the faithful?

sides.position: Only the faithful are searched to the quick; yet the reprobate are still dragged to the tribunal by the word they deride
The truth is all-penetrating in itself, whether preached, read, or pressed home by the Spirit; there can be no escape from it

outliers.note: Alone asks whether the word works this effect on all hearers or only on the faithful, and answers both ways at once — confining the searching to the faithful while insisting the reprobate are still bound, comparing them to furious dogs that bite and claw the chain by which they are held.

Alone assembles a full case against the Christological reading from Pauline usage, disposes of the two texts adduced in its support, and then quotes an authority who grants that every property named here belongs to the Son and still denies that the Logos is meant.

Alone weighs the Alexandrian parallels explicitly, holding that the resemblances to Philo's language about the divine Word cutting through all things are too close to be accidental yet prove familiarity rather than adoption of his system.

themes: For the word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword, piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit, and of the joints and marrow, and is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart.

13.pericope_label: All things are naked and opened unto the eyes of him with whom we have to do

schools.summary: Canvass the readings of the participle and then choose the plainest. The sacrificial derivation is manifestly forced; the criminal reading, first proposed by Erasmus, is equally forced and unnatural; a third view refers it to cutting the animal down the back-bone, adopted on authority that does not in fact support it. The simplest sense is usually best: the word relates to the neck, not the marrow or the skin, and means to bend the neck back so as to expose it when an animal is slain, so that the allusion is to the sword of the previous verse and we are like a beast whose neck is laid bare with nothing to hinder the stroke. Or decline to settle it, since the word is peculiar and the metaphor cannot be determined with certainty: it is usually applied to a wrestler who overthrows his adversary by dragging back the neck, the criminal explanation is attested in Latin authors but not for the Greek word, and there is no good reason to suppose an allusion to a sacrificial victim at all. A sixth picture is available too, the neck bent back as the surgeon does for operating. Then close on the account to be settled, and make it a thought experiment: were we transparent, so that the world could see all we are, who would dare go abroad? The gay multitudes in the streets would become processions of downcast and blushing convicts.

Hold the conjunction causal, the argument drawn from the nature of God himself: nothing is so deep in man's soul that it cannot be drawn into light by the word that resembles its own author, for as it is God's office to search the heart, so he performs that examination by his word. Say that interpreters have strangely perverted the passage for want of seeing that God's word is like a long staff by which he searches what lies deep in our hearts; and that the ambiguity of the last words has led them astray too, since they render them of whom we speak when they ought to be rendered with whom we have to do — so that we should not trifle with him as with a mortal man but tremble whenever his word is set before us. And carry the person of the previous verse forward, applying the omniscience to Christ, who knows the openly profane and the formal professors alike, can distinguish between profession and grace, and observes the springs and progress of apostasy.

Take the phrase as plainly sacrificial, alluding to the victims under the law, first flayed and then laid open. Report the reading in full — the beast slain, flayed and so naked, cut open so that the intestines are exposed, inspected by the priest lest an imperfect offering be made, and split so exactly down the chine that the spinal marrow was cloven down the centre — but then suspect it is not the metaphor here, since the verb signifies to have the neck bent back so as to expose the face, as was often done with criminals that they might be the better recognised; and support that from a panegyric before an emperor, where the informers' upturned faces and twisted necks are a public spectacle. Say also why the word suits the context: God well knew how to construct his word so as to suit it to the state of all hearts, and there is no creature of the affections, mind or imagination that is not constantly under his eye, since he marks every rising thought and every budding desire.

debates.question: What is the metaphor behind the word rendered 'opened'?

sides.position: A sacrificial victim flayed and laid open, the spine cloven down the centre
A criminal whose head is drawn back so that his face may be recognised, as Latin authors describe
An animal whose neck is bent back and laid bare for the knife — the simplest sense, and connected to the sword of the previous verse
It cannot be determined; the word is usually applied to a wrestler dragging back an adversary's neck, and there is no good reason to suppose a sacrificial allusion

debates.question: How should the closing phrase be rendered?

sides.position: With whom we have to do — not 'of whom we speak', a rendering by which interpreters have been led astray
Literally, with whom is our account: the reckoning is with him before whom all is naked and open

outliers.note: Alone reviews every proposed derivation of the participle in turn, names who proposed each, and corrects a misattribution among them before settling on the simplest; and alone turns the verse into a thought experiment about a transparent world whose streets would fill with blushing convicts.

Alone charges other interpreters with perverting the passage, on the ground that they failed to see God's word as a long staff by which he searches what lies deep in us; and alone corrects the rendering of the closing phrase from 'of whom we speak' to 'with whom we have to do'.

Alone records that Luther, Tyndale and Coverdale began the fifth chapter at the verse following this one, and rejects the division on the ground that the connection with what precedes is too close to justify it.

themes: Neither is there any creature that is not manifest in his sight: but all things are naked and opened unto the eyes of him with whom we have to do.

14.pericope_label: A great high priest touched with the feeling of our infirmities

schools.summary: Find all the chief points of the earlier chapters gathered here — the high priesthood, the exaltation, the divine Sonship, the compassion toward the brethren whose lot he came to share — and map the whole book from this verse, Jesus having been shown superior to the prophets, to angels and to Moses, and now to the Levitical line, with five points still to come: a better priest, a better covenant, a better sanctuary, a better sacrifice and better promises. Explain the epithet great from Jewish usage, since in the apostle's time the name belonged also to the deputy, to those who had held the office and retired, and perhaps to the head of each of the twenty-four courses, so that great high priest designates the man actually at the head. Correct the English on the participle: it is not passed into the heavens but passed through them, as the high priest passed through the Holy Place to enter the Holy of Holies. On the sympathy, press that he does not merely show compassion to the suffering but takes to himself a joint feeling of their weaknesses, and that the word must not be limited to pain and bodily suffering but covers whatever belongs to the necessary limitations of the nature he assumed; and note that the beautiful rendering touched with the feeling of our infirmities is owed to a sixteenth-century testament.

Hold that an inference is employed, the writer having referred to this truth before; and supply why the two offices belong together, that the Son sustained a twofold character when sent to us, teacher and priest, the design of both being to enable us to come to God. Having exhorted the Jews to embrace the doctrine of Christ, now show what benefit his priesthood has brought. And draw the thread back rather than forward: this great high priest is no other than the Word of God just spoken of, a priest great because of the dignity of his person, the virtue of his sacrifice, the place where he now officiates and the continuation of his office; and note that the divine Word is often called a priest and a high priest by Philo the Jew.

Settle the particle first: the word we translate seeing should be rendered now, since the apostle, though he had called Christ a high priest twice already, does not attempt to prove it in any preceding chapter but enters on the point here and pursues it for six chapters. Offer a second possibility as well, that the words resume a discourse broken off earlier, all that intervenes being a parenthesis, since the argument then runs on with perfect connection. Supply the objection the passage was written to meet, put by those Jews who wished the Christians of Palestine to apostatize: you have no tabernacle, no temple, no high priest, no sacrifice. Then answer the further objection, that a High Priest entered into the heavens can have no sympathy with us, by conceding more than is comfortable — he sympathizes with our weakness, but his body was perfectly tempered and free from all morbid action, and his human soul, being every way perfect, could feel no irregular temper; in these respects he was different from us, and cannot as man sympathize with us in any feelings of that kind, though as God he has provided support for the body and an atoning sacrifice for the soul.

debates.question: Does this verse draw an inference from what precedes, or open a new argument?

sides.position: A new argument: the particle should be rendered 'now', since the point has been asserted but never proved before this
An inference, the writer having referred to this truth already; the priesthood is fitly joined to the apostleship since both are to bring us to God
A gathering-up: all the chief points of the earlier chapters are brought together here, and the main argument of the Epistle now begins

debates.question: How far does the sympathy of the High Priest extend?

sides.position: To every kind of trial we can face: he was persecuted, poor, despised, and endured the sorrows of a cruel death
Beyond suffering, to whatever belongs to the necessary limitations of the human nature he assumed — a joint feeling of our weaknesses, not mere compassion
Not to everything: his body was perfectly tempered and his soul could feel no irregular temper, so as man he cannot sympathize with us in feelings of that kind

outliers.note: Alone reconstructs the taunt the passage answers — you have no tabernacle, no temple, no high priest, no sacrifice — and alone limits the High Priest's sympathy, holding that a perfectly tempered body and a soul free from irregular temper leave some of our feelings outside what he can share as man.

Alone explains the epithet 'great' from the usage of the time, when the title high priest extended to the deputy, to retired holders of the office and perhaps to the heads of the twenty-four courses, so that the epithet marks the man actually at the head of all.

Alone identifies this great high priest with the Word of God spoken of two verses earlier, carrying his reading of that verse forward, and supports it by noting that Philo often gives the divine Word the title of priest and high priest.

themes: Seeing then that we have a great high priest, that is passed into the heavens, Jesus the Son of God, let us hold fast our profession.
For we have not an high priest which cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities; but was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin.

16.pericope_label: Let us come boldly unto the throne of grace

schools.summary: Build on the temple picture, God seated on the mercy-seat while the great High Priest, having shed his own blood, pleads for the pardon of men, so that we come not on our own merits but where a sufficient sacrifice has been offered. Put pardon first, since we are guilty and self-condemned and our first cry should be for mercy, and he who comes without feeling his need of it must fail of the divine favour; grace comes second, the strength needed even by the forgiven, to keep them from sin in temptation. Or deny that premise: the real meaning may be to receive compassion in our weakness and trials, the thought of obtaining mercy for guilt not being in these words taken by themselves, though grace meets every need — the previous verse having shown that our High Priest knows what help is required, this one assuring us it will be given in the time of need. On the verb, keep it continuous: let us keep on coming to our high priest, making daily use of him instead of deserting him; take boldness to mean telling him the whole story of our shortcomings; and render the last phrase as help in the nick of time.

Draw the conclusion that an access to God is open to all who come relying on Christ the Mediator, and exhort the faithful to venture without hesitation to present themselves before God. Make it a matter of certainty rather than of feeling: the chief benefit of divine teaching is a sure confidence in calling on God, and religion falls to the ground when that certainty is taken from consciences. Hence hold the light of the Gospel extinct where men are bidden to doubt whether God is propitious, and where Christ is confessed a Mediator in words while the power of his priesthood is made of none effect by the anxious seeking of other mediators; for Christ is not really known as a Mediator until all doubt about our access to God is removed. Then rest the comfort on the name the throne is given: it is not arrayed in naked majesty to confound us, for God's glory contemplated alone could only fill us with despair, but is adorned with grace, a name that allures us by its sweetness.

Keep the day of atonement in view and read the throne as its answering piece. The approach is to the propitiatory, the covering of the ark of the testimony with a cherub at each end and between them the symbol of the Divine Majesty; and the superiority of the new covenant over the old lies in who may come. There the high priest only was permitted to approach, with fear and trembling and not without the blood of the victim, and if he transgressed he might expect to be struck with death; here all may approach who feel their need, with freedom and liberty of speech in opposition to that fear. Distinguish the two things asked: mercy refers to the pardon of sin and grace to what supports the soul afterwards; and as Christ tasted death for every man, every man may go to that propitiatory and take mercy suited to his degree of guilt. Then work the etymology of the word for help, which signifies to run at the cry, and turn it into a rule — no help can be expected where there is no cry, and where there is no cry there is no felt necessity, for he that feels he is perishing cries aloud, and to such a cry the compassionate High Priest runs. Nor is the timing indifferent: we are not to cry to day to be helped to morrow, or at the hour of death, but to call when we need mercy and grace and to expect them when we call.

debates.question: Does 'that we may obtain mercy' mean pardon for guilt?

sides.position: Yes, and it is the first thing asked: we are guilty and self-condemned, and mercy means the pardon of sin and being brought into God's favour
No: the real meaning is to receive compassion in our weakness and trials; the thought of mercy for guilt is not in these words taken by themselves

debates.question: Whom does the believer come to at the throne of grace?

sides.position: To the high priest himself: instead of deserting him, let us make daily use of him
To God, access being open to all who come relying on Christ the Mediator
Either to Christ, who was typified by the mercy seat, or else to the Father, since Christ is the way of access

outliers.note: Alone works the etymology of the word for help, which means to run at the cry, into a rule of prayer — that no help can be expected where there is no cry, and no cry comes where necessity is not felt — and alone insists on the timing, that we are not to cry to day to be helped to morrow or at the hour of death.

Alone turns the verse into a controversy, holding the light of the Gospel extinct wherever men are bidden to doubt whether God is propitious to them and other mediators are anxiously sought; and alone rests the comfort on the throne's name, which is not naked majesty, since God's glory contemplated alone could only fill us with despair.
Alone denies that mercy here means pardon for guilt, holding the real sense to be compassion received in our weakness and trials, with grace left to meet every need.

themes: Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy, and find grace to help in time of need.
